title: Spectral Unlearning: Transformer Structure-Preserving Updates for Language Models
claim: Matrix-structured spectral updates reach low unlearning objective far faster than entry-wise optimizers, in both steps and wall-clock time.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots sharing y-axis, legend grouped by update type
description: Two side-by-side line charts share a y-axis labeled 'Unlearning objective' (0 to 20). Panel (a) plots objective against unlearning steps (0 to 120). Panel (b) plots it against wall-clock time in minutes (0 to 6). Dashed gray and gold curves, labeled as entry-wise updates (NPO-AdamW, NPO-Sophia), decay slowly and plateau at about 4 and 1.7. Solid teal, purple and red curves, labeled as spectral updates (SU-NPO-Muon, SU-NPO-KLShampoo, SU-NPO-SOAP), drop sharply and approach about 1. A dotted black horizontal line marks the retain-model target near 0.6. Shaded bands show variance. A boxed legend in panel (a) groups the methods into 'Entry-wise update' and 'Spectral update'. Bold subtitles read '(a) Objective vs. steps' and '(b) Objective vs. time'. The eye goes first to the steep solid curves.
caption: The Llama-3.2-1B model forgets data from the TOFU benchmark through the negative preference optimization (NPO) unlearning method. Loss curves are plotted against (a) unlearning steps and (b) wall-clock time. Dashed curves use conventional entry-wise updates. Solid curves use our proposed spectral update (SU), realized through Muon, KLShampoo, and SOAP.
abstract: Machine unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specific learned knowledge, capabilities, or behaviors while preserving model utility. Existing methods have mostly focused on the design of unlearning objectives, while largely overlooking the intrinsic matrix structure of transformer weights. In particular, standard optimizers operate on independent scalar coordinates, thereby ignoring this matrix structure. We propose spectral unlearning, an update framework that combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured optimization. We show that the spectral update corresponds to the steepest-descent direction for transformers composed of linear layers with normalized inputs and outputs. Our approach is applied on top of existing unlearning methods and evaluated across complementary axes of memorization, privacy, and utility, summarized via their harmonic mean. Spectral unlearning consistently outperforms a broad range of baselines and closes most of the gap to a retain-trained reference. Code is available at https://github.com/unlearn-ml/spectral-unlearning/.
